name: Josep Lluís Sert
bio:
Josep Lluís Sert (1902–1983) was a Catalan architect and urban planner who worked for Le Corbusier in Paris and co-founded GATCPAC, the group that brought modern architecture to Barcelona in the 1930s. For the 1937 Paris Exposition he designed the Spanish Republic's pavilion, which showed Picasso's Guernica. After Franco's victory he went into exile in the United States, was president of CIAM from 1947 to 1956, and served as dean of the Harvard Graduate School of Design from 1953 to 1969.

In Barcelona, Casa Bloc (1936) was one of the first steps towards decent housing for workers and is now a symbol of the city's rationalist architecture. His close friendships with artists shaped two museums. The Fondation Maeght in Saint-Paul-de-Vence (1964) follows the slope of its site in terraces of galleries, patios and gardens, lit by half-vaulted roofs that catch and spread daylight. The Fundació Joan Miró (1975) stands on Montjuïc in Barcelona. At Harvard he designed the Holyoke Center (1966) and brought Le Corbusier to build the Carpenter Center. Josep Lluís Sert's work is studied for modernism made for climate, art and city life.

name: Kim Swoo-geun
bio:
Kim Swoo-geun (1931–1986) was a South Korean architect, teacher and publisher, counted with Kim Chung-up among the key figures of modern Korean architecture. He studied architecture in Tokyo during the Korean War, founded his own office in 1961, the forerunner of today's SPACE Group, and taught at Hongik University. In 1966 he started SPACE, South Korea's first general art journal, and he backed so many art forms that TIME called him the "Lorenzo de Medici of Seoul" in 1977. Colleagues said his lifelong concern was how to carry Korean tradition into contemporary architecture.

The Buyeo National Museum (1967) and Sewoon Sangga in Seoul (1967) come from his first decade. The Space Group Building in Seoul (1977), his own office, also held a small theatre and gallery that became important stages for Korean culture. Yangdeok Cathedral in Changwon (1979) and Kyungdong Presbyterian Church in Seoul (1981) are among his best-known churches. The Seoul Olympic Stadium (1984), built for the 1986 Asian Games and the 1988 Olympics, takes its profile from the curves of Joseon white porcelain. Kim Swoo-geun's buildings are studied for joining Korean tradition to modern design.

name: Minoru Yamasaki
bio:
Minoru Yamasaki (1912–1986) was an American architect, born in Seattle to Japanese immigrant parents, best known for the original World Trade Center in New York, designed from 1962 with Emery Roth & Sons. Many of his buildings carry details drawn from pointed Gothic arches and very narrow vertical windows, a style that grew partly from his own fear of heights. Two of his major projects, the Pruitt–Igoe housing in St. Louis and the World Trade Center, were destroyed on live television; the historian Charles Jencks saw Pruitt–Igoe's demolition as the symbolic end of modernist architecture.

The McGregor Memorial Conference Center in Detroit (1958) stands on a raised base, with repeated geometric patterns on its façade, white marble and a skylight running its whole length. His terminal at Dhahran Air Terminal in Saudi Arabia (1961) was so well received that it appeared on the one-riyal banknote. The Pacific Science Center in Seattle (1962), built for the World's Fair, was his first widely acclaimed design. After criticism of the dramatic cantilever of Rainier Tower in Seattle (1977), he became less adventurous. Minoru Yamasaki's buildings are studied for ornament and pattern within modernism.

name: Morphosis
bio:
Morphosis is an architecture and design practice based in Los Angeles and New York City, founded informally in 1972 by Michael Brickler, Thom Mayne, Livio Santini and James Stafford; Michael Rotondi was a principal from 1975 to 1991. Thom Mayne, its leading figure, was a founding member of the Southern California Institute of Architecture (SCI-Arc) and won the Pritzker Prize in 2005.

The Graduate House, University of Toronto (2000) and Diamond Ranch High School in Pomona (2000) come from its rise in the 1990s. The San Francisco Federal Building (2007) uses daylight for 80 percent of its space, and its south wall of perforated stainless-steel panels warms in the sun to pull cool air through sensor-controlled windows; it was the first federal building certified under LEED. 41 Cooper Square in New York (2009) wraps a full-height atrium in an operable skin of perforated stainless steel. The Perot Museum of Nature and Science in Dallas (2012) is a large cube floating over a landscaped base, with an escalator in a glass tube slanting outside it. Morphosis's projects are studied for layered building skins and climate-driven design.

name: Nikken Sekkei
bio:
Nikken Sekkei is a Japanese architecture and engineering practice that traces its origins to 1900, when it began as the building department of the Sumitomo company to design the firm's headquarters. It became independent in the 1950s, has been owned partly by its own employees since 1970, and by 2019 ranked as the second-largest architectural practice in the world. Its long list of works includes Tokyo Tower (1958) and Tokyo Dome (1988).

Kobe Port Tower (1963), 108 metres high, is shaped like a tsuzumi, a Japanese hand drum, and was the first tower built of a steel pipe lattice. The Shinjuku NS Building in Tokyo (1982) and the Cairo Opera House (1988) followed. Nikken Sekkei was the main architect of Tokyo Skytree (2012), a 634-metre broadcasting tower that on completion was the tallest tower in the world. One Za'abeel in Dubai (2023) continues its work on very tall buildings. Nikken Sekkei's projects are studied for how a large practice joins architecture and structural engineering on very big and very tall buildings.

name: Rogelio Salmona
bio:
Rogelio Salmona (1929–2007) was a French-Colombian architect, born in Paris and raised in Bogotá, known for red brick and for spirals, curves and radial plans drawn from nature. Invited by Le Corbusier during his 1947 visit to Colombia, he worked as a draughtsman in Le Corbusier's Paris studio for about ten years, and the brickwork he saw in Granada had a lasting influence on him. Late in life he won the Alvar Aalto Medal (2003).

His first major project, Torres del Parque in Bogotá (1970), is a group of three brick residential towers around a park at the centre of the city. The General Archive of the Nation (1994) and the Gabriel García Márquez Cultural Center (2008) are also in Bogotá, and the Centro Cultural de Cali (1990) in the south-west of the country. The Virgilio Barco Library (2001), set in Bogotá's Simón Bolívar Metropolitan Park, is noted for its handling of water, with pools around the building; it is one of seven sites Colombia has put forward to UNESCO as "The architectural legacy of Rogelio Salmona". Rogelio Salmona's buildings are studied for brick, landscape and public space.

name: Sou Fujimoto
bio:
Sou Fujimoto (born 1971) is a Japanese architect from Hokkaido, known for delicate, light structures and enclosures that are permeable to light, air and views. He graduated from the University of Tokyo in 1994 and opened Sou Fujimoto Architects in 2000. His 2008 book, Primitive Future, surveys his early projects and explains the idea behind them. In 2013 he designed the Serpentine Gallery Pavilion in London, and he designed the Grand Ring for the Osaka Expo.

His early houses in Japan made his name. Final Wooden House in Kumamoto (2008) grew from his winning entry to a 2005 wooden house competition, and House N in Oita (2008) followed the same year. In 2014 he designed a bus shelter for the BUS:STOP project in Krumbach, Austria. Larger works followed in Europe: L'Arbre Blanc in Montpellier (2019), a tower of flats, and the House of Music Hungary in Budapest (2022). Sou Fujimoto's projects are studied for light, open structures that blur the line between inside and outside.

name: Victor Horta
bio:
Victor Horta (1861–1947) was a Belgian architect and designer, one of the founders of the Art Nouveau movement and a forerunner of modern architecture through his open plans and his use of iron, steel and glass. An admirer of the French theorist Viollet-le-Duc, he first worked with glass and iron on the Royal Greenhouses of Laeken. In 2000 four of his Brussels town houses were listed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, praised for "their open plan, the diffusion of light" and the joining of curved decoration with structure.

The Autrique House (1893) came just before the Hôtel Tassel (1894), often called the first Art Nouveau house, where slender iron columns carry a large bay window. The Hôtel van Eetvelde (1898) and his own Horta House (1901), now the Horta Museum, followed. Later he moved to a more geometric, Art Deco-influenced style: at the Centre for Fine Arts (Bozar) in Brussels (1928), reinforced concrete let him shape a horseshoe-shaped concert hall. Brussels-Central Station, delayed by economic trouble and war, was finished in 1952. Victor Horta's houses are studied for light, open plans and structure joined to ornament.

name: Yoshio Taniguchi
bio:
Yoshio Taniguchi (1937–2024) was a Japanese architect best known for his redesign of the Museum of Modern Art in New York, and for calm, exact museums that join traditional Japanese aesthetics with modernism. The son of the architect Yoshirō Taniguchi, he studied engineering at Keio University and architecture at Harvard, worked briefly for Walter Gropius and from 1964 to 1972 for Kenzō Tange, and opened his own office in Tokyo in 1975.

Most of his work is museums in Japan, among them the Ken Domon Museum of Photography in Sakata (1983), the Marugame Genichiro-Inokuma Museum of Contemporary Art (MIMOCA) (1991), the Toyota Municipal Museum of Art (1995) and the Gallery of Horyuji Treasures at the Tokyo National Museum (1999). In 1997 he beat nine international architects, among them Rem Koolhaas and Herzog & de Meuron, to redesign the Museum of Modern Art (2004), his first work outside Japan; its central atrium, his "light garden", helps visitors find their way "visually, not with signs". The D. T. Suzuki Museum in Kanazawa (2011) looks over a still Water Mirror Garden. Yoshio Taniguchi's buildings are studied for clarity, proportion and calm.

name: 3XN
bio:
3XN is a Danish architecture practice headquartered in Copenhagen, with offices in Stockholm, London, New York and Sydney. It was founded in Aarhus in 1986 as Nielsen, Nielsen & Nielsen by Kim Herforth Nielsen, Hans Peter Svendler Nielsen and Lars Frank Nielsen, and is now led by five senior partners with Kim Herforth Nielsen as creative director. Its international breakthrough came in the late 1990s with the Danish Embassy in Berlin and the competition for the Muziekgebouw in Amsterdam.

The Muziekgebouw aan 't IJ in Amsterdam (2005) is Amsterdam's main hall for contemporary classical music, built over the IJ tunnel. Ørestad Gymnasium in Copenhagen (2007) turns four boomerang-shaped floors around one another to make a school of open study spaces instead of closed classrooms. The Bella Sky Hotel in Copenhagen (2011) is two towers, 76.5 metres high, leaning 15 degrees in opposite directions. Den Blå Planet (National Aquarium Denmark) (2013) and Quay Quarter Tower in Sydney (2022) are among its later works. 3XN's projects are studied for how a building's form can shape the way people meet and learn.

name: Arthur Erickson
bio:
Arthur Erickson (1924–2009) was a Canadian architect and urban planner from Vancouver, seen as one of the most influential architects in Canada and the only Canadian to win the AIA Gold Medal. In 1962 he founded Erickson/Massey Architects with Geoffrey Massey, and his buildings often drew on the post-and-beam building of the Pacific Coast First Nations, Asian temples and the log cabin.

Simon Fraser University (1965), the campus he and Massey won in a 1963 competition, sits on top of Burnaby Mountain in raw concrete that matches the land in colour but not in shape. The MacMillan Bloedel Building in Vancouver (1968), which he called "a Doric building in its starkness", is a 27-storey concrete tower of two offset halves with deeply recessed windows. The Museum of Anthropology at UBC (1976) joins reinforced concrete to post-and-beam construction, with huge beams, concrete piers and long walls of glass. Robson Square in Vancouver (1983), a three-block civic centre of plazas, waterfalls and ramped stairs, was designed with the landscape architect Cornelia Oberlander. Arthur Erickson's buildings are studied for concrete, landscape and their response to the Pacific coast.

name: Erich Mendelsohn
bio:
Erich Mendelsohn (1887–1953) was a German-British architect known for the expressionist architecture of the 1920s and for the "dynamic functionalism" of his department stores and cinemas. His Mossehaus of 1921 made him a pioneer of Art Deco and Streamline Moderne. Born to a Jewish family in Allenstein, East Prussia, he fled Germany for England in 1933 as the Nazis rose, opened an office in Jerusalem in 1935, and settled in San Francisco in 1945.

The Einstein Tower in Potsdam (1921), built to house a solar telescope for testing Einstein's theory of relativity, was meant as sculpture in reinforced concrete, though it was built partly of brick; it is still a working observatory. The Schocken Department Store in Chemnitz (1930) is known for its curved front with long horizontal strips of windows. In England, with Serge Chermayeff, he designed the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill-on-Sea (1935), described by Historic England as the UK's first modernist public building. In Jerusalem he built the Schocken Library (1936) and the Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus (1939). Erich Mendelsohn's buildings are studied for the expression of movement in curves and long horizontal bands.

name: Gio Ponti
bio:
Gio Ponti (1891–1979) was an Italian architect, industrial and furniture designer, artist, teacher, writer and publisher from Milan. In 1928 he founded the magazine Domus, which he edited for most of his life, and through it and the Milan Triennial he championed Italian design. His Superleggera chair, made by Cassina from 1957, is a classic of Italian design.

The Torre Branca in Milan (1933), first called the Littoria Tower, is a 108-metre steel tower. His best-known building, the Pirelli Tower in Milan (1960), was designed with the engineer Pier Luigi Nervi: 127 metres and 32 storeys, with a structural skeleton, curtain walls and tapered sides, it was among the first skyscrapers to give up the usual block form. In Caracas he designed one of his masterpieces, the Villa Planchart (Quinta El Cerrito) (1957), a house conceived as a work of art in a tropical garden. The Co-Cathedral of the Great Mother of God (Gran Madre di Dio) in Taranto (1970) is crowned by a tall concrete screen pierced with openings, known locally as "the sail". Gio Ponti's work is studied for joining architecture, furniture and decoration.

name: Gottfried Böhm
bio:
Gottfried Böhm (1920–2021) was a German architect and sculptor, the son of the church architect Dominikus Böhm, known for highly sculptural buildings in concrete, steel and glass. In 1986 he became the first German architect to win the Pritzker Prize. His earlier projects were mostly in moulded concrete; later, as both materials advanced, he used more steel and glass. His first independent building was the Cologne chapel "Madonna in the Rubble", now part of Peter Zumthor's Kolumba museum.

His most influential and best-known building is the Neviges Pilgrimage Church in Velbert (1968), dedicated to Mary, Queen of Peace. Bensberg Town Hall (1969) and the church of Christi Auferstehung in Cologne (1970) come from the same years of sculptural concrete, followed by the Diözesanmuseum Paderborn (1975). He was still at work in his eighties and nineties, with the Hans Otto Theater in Potsdam (2006) and the Cologne Central Mosque, completed in 2018. Gottfried Böhm's buildings are studied for treating concrete as sculpture at the scale of a building.

name: Henning Larsen
bio:
Henning Larsen (1925–2013) was a Danish architect, internationally known for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Riyadh and the Copenhagen Opera House. He studied at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts, the Architectural Association in London and MIT, counted Arne Jacobsen and Jørn Utzon among his mentors, and taught at the Royal Danish Academy from 1968 to 1995. His practice, Henning Larsen Architects, has continued under his name since his death. He won the Aga Khan Award for the Riyadh ministry in 1989 and the Praemium Imperiale in 2012.

The Copenhagen Opera House (2005) was designed in close and often difficult collaboration with the shipping magnate Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller, who paid for it. Harpa in Reykjavík (2011), a concert hall and conference centre, has a coloured glass façade inspired by Iceland's basalt landscape that also carries light works by the artist Olafur Eliasson. Bolgen in Vejle (2009) and Bildmuseet in Umeå (2012), clad in larch that will fade to grey, are among the practice's later works. Henning Larsen's buildings are studied for daylight and for civic buildings set into their landscape.

name: Kiyonori Kikutake
bio:
Kiyonori Kikutake (1928–2011) was a Japanese architect from Kurume and one of the founders of the Metabolist group. He is best known for Marine City (1958), a proposal for a floating city that became part of the Metabolist manifesto launched at the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo. He taught and employed several important architects, including Toyo Ito and Itsuko Hasegawa, worked on more than 40 buildings with the structural engineer Gengo Matsui, and received the UIA Auguste Perret Prize in 1978.

His own Sky House in Tokyo (1958) and the Hotel Tokoen in Yonago (1964) were designed with Matsui. The Edo-Tokyo Museum (1993) lifts seven floors 62 metres into the air on four great columns over an open plaza; its form comes from the traditional raised rice storehouse, and Kikutake said it "crystallizes Japanese culture in built form". The Shimane Art Museum (1999), the National Showa Memorial Museum in Tokyo (1999) and the Kyushu National Museum in Dazaifu (2005) are among his later public buildings. Kiyonori Kikutake's work is studied for Metabolist ideas of growth and change, and for big structures inspired by Japanese tradition.

name: Konstantin Melnikov
bio:
Konstantin Melnikov (1890–1974) was a Russian architect and painter whose bold workers' clubs, garages and house made him one of the leading figures of the Soviet avant-garde of the 1920s. Though often grouped with the Constructivists, he was an independent artist who kept his distance from their group. In 1925 he designed the Soviet pavilion at the Paris decorative arts exhibition. In the 1930s he refused to conform to Stalinist architecture, withdrew from practice, and worked as a portrait painter and teacher for the rest of his life.

His workers' clubs could be divided into separate halls: the main hall of the Rusakov Workers' Club in Moscow (1928) splits into three. Melnikov House on Krivoarbatsky Lane (1929), his own home and finest surviving work, is two interlocking cylinders pierced by a pattern of hexagonal windows. For Moscow's buses and trucks he designed the Bakhmetevsky Bus Garage (1928), with an unusual parallelogram plan and a roof by the engineer Vladimir Shukhov, and the horseshoe-shaped Novo-Ryazanskaya Street Bus Garage (1929). Konstantin Melnikov's buildings are studied for original geometry and for plans that could change with use.

name: Louis Sullivan
bio:
Louis Sullivan (1856–1924) was an American architect called a "father of skyscrapers" and a "father of modernism". A leading figure of the Chicago School and mentor to Frank Lloyd Wright, he is credited with the phrase "form follows function", which became a central idea of modern architecture. He partnered with the engineer Dankmar Adler from 1880.

The Wainwright Building in St. Louis (1891), was called by Wright "the very first human expression of a tall steel office-building as Architecture". His tall buildings were spare in their main forms but broken by bursts of Art Nouveau or Celtic Revival ornament, often cast in iron or terracotta. The Bayard–Condict Building in New York (1899) is his only building in the city. Late in life he designed a series of small Midwestern banks, his "Jewel Boxes", among them the National Farmers' Bank of Owatonna (1908) and the Home Building Association Bank in Newark, Ohio (1914). The Krause Music Store in Chicago (1922) was the last of his 126 buildings. Louis Sullivan's buildings are studied for the tall office building and for ornament grown from nature.

name: Mahendra Raj
bio:
Mahendra Raj (1924–2022) was an Indian structural engineer whose solutions for exposed concrete made possible many of the boldest buildings of post-independence India. Born in Gujranwala, he studied civil engineering in Lahore, moved to India at Partition in 1947, and as a young engineer worked with Le Corbusier on the High Court and Secretariat at Chandigarh. After a master's degree at the University of Minnesota and work in New York, he founded his own consultancy in Bombay in 1960. Over six decades he worked on more than 250 projects with architects including B. V. Doshi, Charles Correa and Raj Rewal.

With Correa he built the Hindustan Lever pavilion in New Delhi (1961), sprayed concrete folded like a crumpled sheet of paper. The Shri Ram Centre for Performing Arts in New Delhi (1969) and Akbar Bhawan (Akbar Hotel) (1970) were designed with Shiv Nath Prasad. The Hall of Nations at Pragati Maidan in New Delhi (1972), designed with Raj Rewal, was one of the largest space-frame structures in the world, which the New York Times called a "brutalist masterpiece". Mahendra Raj's work is studied for how engineers shape architecture.

name: Michael Wilford
bio:
Michael Wilford (1938–2023) was an English architect who joined James Stirling's office in 1960 and became his partner in 1971; the Stirling/Wilford partnership lasted until Stirling's death in 1992. Wilford then led his own practices, Michael Wilford and Partners in Britain and Wilford Schupp in Stuttgart, designing performing arts centres, galleries, museums and libraries around the world. He taught at Yale, Harvard, Rice and many other schools, and was made a CBE in 2001.

With Stirling he designed the Clore Gallery, Tate Britain in London (1987) and the Stuttgart Music School (Musikhochschule) (1996). After Stirling's death he completed No 1 Poultry in London (1997). The Lowry in Salford (2000), a performing and visual arts centre largely clad in stainless steel and glass, won the Royal Fine Art Commission Building of the Year award in 2001. His practice also worked, with DP Architects, on Esplanade - Theatres on the Bay in Singapore (2002), whose two glass shells covered in more than 7,000 aluminium sunshades earned it the nickname "the Durian". Michael Wilford's buildings are studied for colourful public architecture made for crowds.

name: Nicholas Grimshaw
bio:
Nicholas Grimshaw (1939–2025) was an English architect and one of the pioneers of high-tech architecture, best known for Waterloo International railway station and the Eden Project. He named the 19th-century engineers Joseph Paxton and Isambard Kingdom Brunel among his influences, alongside Buckminster Fuller and Charles and Ray Eames. He was president of the Royal Academy from 2004 to 2011 and was knighted.

Waterloo International in London (1993), the terminal for trains to mainland Europe, was named RIBA President's Building of the Year in 1994. The Eden Project in Cornwall (2001), built in a reclaimed china clay pit, grows rainforest and Mediterranean plants inside biomes of hexagonal and pentagonal ETFE cushions on geodesic steel domes, a clear debt to Fuller. The National Space Centre in Leicester (2001) houses upright rockets in a 42-metre tower clad in the same inflated ETFE. Southern Cross Station in Melbourne (2006) continued his practice's work on large stations. Nicholas Grimshaw's projects are studied for lightweight structure and the engineering of large spans.

name: RCR Arquitectes
bio:
RCR Arquitectes is a Catalan architecture practice founded in Olot, Spain, by Rafael Aranda, Carme Pigem and Ramon Vilalta, who grew up in the town and graduated together from the Vallès School of Architecture in 1987. The practice is known for its frequent use of weathering steel. In 2017 the three received the Pritzker Prize, the first time three architects shared it, though they were then less known than the other finalists.

The Sant Antoni-Joan Oliver Library in Barcelona (2007) is one of their works in the city. The Soulages Museum in Rodez, France (2014) came from a competition the practice won in 2007. De Krook in Ghent, Belgium (2017), a public library and media centre designed with the local firm Coussée & Goris, takes its name from the bend of the river Scheldt that wraps around its site. RCR's buildings are studied for the way a single material and a careful reading of the ground can carry a whole design.

name: Ricardo Legorreta
bio:
Ricardo Legorreta (1931–2011) was a Mexican architect who designed houses, public buildings and master plans across Mexico, the United States and beyond. Born in Mexico City, he graduated from the National Autonomous University of Mexico in 1953 and worked for ten years with José Villagrán García before opening his own office in 1963. A follower of Luis Barragán, he carried Barragán's bright colour, play of light and shadow and solid geometric forms from houses into hotels, factories, offices and schools. He received the UIA Gold Medal in 1999, the AIA Gold Medal in 2000 and the Praemium Imperiale in 2011.

The Camino Real Hotel, Mexico City (1968) is among his best-known works, as is the Metropolitan Cathedral of Managua (1993) in Nicaragua. The Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Monterrey (1991) has eleven gallery halls and a central courtyard with a water mirror. The Papalote Children's Museum (1993) in Mexico City uses geometric figures and traditional Mexican tiles, and in the United States he designed the San Antonio Central Library (1995). His Fashion and Textile Museum (2003) in London is a converted warehouse coloured hot pink, orange, yellow and blue.

name: Richard Neutra
bio:
Richard Neutra (1892–1970) was an Austrian-American architect who worked for most of his career in Southern California and became one of its leading modernists. Born in Vienna, he studied at the Vienna University of Technology and at Adolf Loos's private school, worked for Erich Mendelsohn in Berlin, and reached the United States by 1923, working briefly for Frank Lloyd Wright before joining his friend Rudolf Schindler in California. He sometimes gave clients detailed questionnaires about how they lived, and wrote books including Survival Through Design (1954). He was awarded the AIA Gold Medal after his death, in 1977.

The Jardinette Apartments (1928) in Los Angeles were his first American commission. The Lovell Health House (1929) is often described as the first steel-frame house in the United States. For his own home, the VDL Research House (1932), he set out to bring the ideas of the Lovell house to less wealthy clients. The Kaufmann Desert House (1946) in Palm Springs was built for Edgar J. Kaufmann, who had commissioned Fallingwater, and the small Constance Perkins House (1955) in Pasadena was scaled to its owner.

name: Ryue Nishizawa
bio:
Ryue Nishizawa (born 1966) is a Japanese architect based in Tokyo. A graduate of Yokohama National University, he co-founded SANAA with Kazuyo Sejima in 1995 and set up his own practice, the Office of Ryue Nishizawa, in 1997. In 2010 he and Sejima received the Pritzker Prize, and at 44 he became its youngest winner.

His own projects include the Moriyama House in Tokyo (2005). The Towada Art Center (2008) opened as part of a project to revive the city of Towada, and the Teshima Art Museum (2010), on an island in Japan's Seto Inland Sea, is a single concrete shell 25 centimetres thick, 40 by 60 metres and four metres high at most, holding one work by the artist Rei Naito. He later completed the Hiroshi Senju Museum Karuizawa (2011) and the Garden & House in Tokyo (2011). With Sejima, as SANAA, he designed the New Museum in New York (2007), a stack of white boxes on the Bowery. Ryue Nishizawa's work is studied for thin structure and spaces that blur inside and out.

name: Snøhetta
bio:
Snøhetta is an architecture and landscape practice founded in Oslo, Norway, and named after a mountain in the Dovrefjell range. It grew from a group of architects and landscape architects, including Kjetil Trædal Thorsen and Craig Dykers, who shared an office in Oslo from 1987 and wanted architecture and landscape treated as a single idea. In 1989 they entered the open competition for the new Bibliotheca Alexandrina in Egypt, which they went on to build; it was completed in 2001.

The Oslo Opera House (2008) is clad in white granite and Carrara marble, and its sloping roof comes down to the water as a plaza people can walk up; it won the Mies van der Rohe Award. Lascaux IV in Montignac, France (2016), holds a full-scale replica of the painted cave on the same hill as the original. The Calgary Central Library in Canada (2018), designed with the Canadian firm DIALOG, is entered under wood-clad arches inspired by the cloud arches of Chinook winds. Under (2019) in Lindesnes, Norway, has a dining room 5.5 metres below sea level and is the largest underwater restaurant in the world.

name: Sverre Fehn
bio:
Sverre Fehn (1924–2009) was a Norwegian architect who designed more than 100 buildings, many of them museums and houses. Born in Kongsberg, he studied in Oslo under Arne Korsmo, discovered the vernacular architecture of Morocco on travels in 1952–53, and worked for two years in Paris in the studio of Jean Prouvé before opening his own office in Oslo in 1954. He taught at the Oslo School of Architecture from 1971 to 1995 and received the Pritzker Prize in 1997.

The Nordic Pavilion at the Venice Biennale (1962) was designed to let in light like that of the Nordic countries. Villa Schreiner in Oslo (1963) and Villa Busk in Bamble (1990) are among his houses. At the Hedmark Museum in Hamar (1979) he built in concrete, wood and glass inside a 17th-century barn beside medieval ruins, with ramps for viewing the museum. Later came the Norwegian Glacier Museum at Fjærland (1991), which he extended in the 2000s, and the National Museum – Architecture in Oslo (2008). Sverre Fehn's buildings are studied for how new work meets old.

name: Alejandro Aravena
bio:
Alejandro Aravena (born 1967) is a Chilean architect and executive director of ELEMENTAL, a practice known for social housing that residents finish and extend themselves. He graduated from the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile in 1992, studied in Venice, and founded his own office in 1994. He taught at Harvard from 2000 to 2005 and became ELEMENTAL's executive director in 2006. In 2016 he received the Pritzker Prize and directed the Venice Architecture Biennale, "Reporting from the Front".

Quinta Monroy in Iquique (2004) built 93 homes for families who had occupied the site since the 1960s, giving each a "half a house" with a kitchen and bathroom and leaving the other half for them to build. ELEMENTAL took the same approach in Monterrey Housing (2010) in Mexico and in Villa Verde Housing (2013) in Constitución. At the Catholic University in Santiago he designed the leaning Siamese Towers (2005), and he also designed the Anacleto Angelini Innovation Center (2014). Alejandro Aravena's projects are studied for what architecture can do with a fixed and tight budget.

name: Clorindo Testa
bio:
Clorindo Testa (1923–2013) was an Italian-born Argentine architect and painter, one of the leaders of Argentine rationalism and a pioneer of brutalism in the country. Born in Benevento, near Naples, he came to architecture through naval and civil engineering and graduated from the University of Buenos Aires in 1948; after two years in Europe he also became a painter. Colour, tension and sculptural form run through his buildings, and he won Argentina's Konex Award for visual arts three times.

In the 1950s he began the government centre in Santa Rosa, La Pampa Civic Centre (Casa de Gobierno) (1963). The Bank of London and South America in Buenos Aires (1966), designed by Testa within the SEPRA firm, set an exposed concrete structure among Beaux-Arts neighbours and changed how Argentine banks were built. The National Library of Argentina, designed with Francisco Bullrich and Alicia Cazzaniga in 1961, was begun only in 1971 and opened in 1992. Later works in Buenos Aires include the Hospital Naval Pedro Mallo (1981) and the Recoleta Cultural Center (1980). Clorindo Testa's buildings are studied for brutalism as sculpture.

name: Denton Corker Marshall
bio:
Denton Corker Marshall is an architecture practice founded in Melbourne, Australia, in 1972 by John Denton, Bill Corker and Barrie Marshall. Melbourne remains its design base, with further offices in London, Manchester and Jakarta, and it has worked on more than 510 projects in 37 countries. Its Australian work has been described as modernist, minimalist, sculptural and heroic, and "blades" and sticks became its hallmarks.

In Melbourne, the Melbourne Exhibition Centre ('Jeff's Shed') (1996), nicknamed after the state premier Jeff Kennett, is a long shed entered under one of the practice's blades, and the Melbourne Museum (2000) in the Carlton Gardens is led by two long, high, sloping canopies that guide visitors in. In Sydney the practice designed Governor Phillip Tower (1993) and the Museum of Sydney (1995). The Manchester Civil Justice Centre (2007) in England, nicknamed the "filing cabinet" for the floors cantilevered at its ends, carries a suspended glass wall 60 by 60 metres. Denton Corker Marshall's buildings are studied for bold structure in large public buildings.
